title: Humming first
hook: hum quietly with a recording before trying the words

segments.voice: Yesterday, listening with the words, following a shabad line by line. Your line was sound and sense together. Did the words and music lock, even once? Day one hundred nine.
screen: `LISTENING WITH THE WORDS — SOUND AND SENSE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Be honest. When was the last time you sang out loud where someone could hear you? For a lot of adults, the answer is happy birthday, badly, at the back of the group. Somewhere along the way we decided singing belongs to people with good voices, and the rest of us should keep quiet. And yet. Watch someone washing dishes alone, or a parent rocking a baby at two in the morning, or a person waiting at a crosswalk with earbuds in. Many of them are humming. No words, no audience, nobody judging. Humming is the singing we do before we remember to be embarrassed. That's exactly where kirtan starts.
screen: `WHEN DID YOU LAST SING ALOUD?` → `DISHES, A BABY, A CROSSWALK.` → `SINGING BEFORE EMBARRASSMENT.`

segments.voice: Five days of listening. Now five days of singing, and the first one doesn't use words at all. Humming first. It's how many kirtan teachers start a nervous beginner, and it's how children in Sikh homes often learn a shabad before they can read it. You put on a recording, and you hum along under it, quietly, following the tune. Why start there? Three reasons. First, the melody. A shabad's tune can wander, following its raag, and it's hard to learn the notes and the words at the same time. Humming lets you learn the road before you carry anything down it. Second, the fear. Humming is almost impossible to do badly. Nobody's listening for your pronunciation. Your voice gets used to joining in, without the pressure of getting it right. Third, the body. When you hum, you can feel it in your chest and face. The music stops being something outside you and becomes something happening inside you. That matters, because the Gurus never meant kirtan to be a performance for an audience. In the Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: sing, and listen, and keep love in your mind, and sorrow will leave, and peace will come home. Notice: sing and listen, together. Not sing well. Nobody is grading a hum. Kirtan in the gurdwara is often led by trained musicians called ragis, but the sangat has always joined in. The Gurus' hymns are meant to be in ordinary mouths. Yours included. Start with a hum.
screen: `FIVE DAYS OF SINGING BEGIN.` · `LEARN THE ROAD FIRST.` · `A HUM CAN'T BE WRONG.` · `SING, LISTEN, KEEP LOVE IN MIND.` · then, large: `HUM FIRST.`

segments.voice: Put on a shabad you heard this week, or any gentle tune you know. Sit comfortably. Close your mouth and breathe through your nose. Now hum along with it, very softly, just under the recording. Don't worry about the right notes. Feel the buzz in your lips, your chest, the bones of your face. If you lose the tune, just listen until you find it again, then join back in. Keep humming, softly, all the way through. The bell holds the time.
Humming first. Joining a shabad's melody without words, so the tune, and your voice, get ready before the words arrive.
Your line: hum first. Today, hum one tune while you do something ordinary: the dishes, the walk, the wait. Day one hundred nine.

howItsDone: Many children in Sikh homes learn shabads by humming and singing along with recordings or with family, and kirtan teachers often have beginners learn a tune before its words.
